did_you_know.text: Did you know? Psalm 78 is headed “A Maskil of Asaph”—a teaching psalm that calls the people to listen to its instruction and words of wisdom.
Did you know? The psalmist emphasizes that the message rests on a tradition passed down from parents to children: “What we have heard and known, what our fathers have told us.”
Did you know? The purpose of passing these stories on to the next generation is twofold: to trust in God and remember his deeds, while also keeping his commandments.

Did you know? The people of Ephraim are described in the psalm as warriors who carried bows but turned back on the day of battle; this serves as an example of unfaithfulness and failure to stand the test.
Did you know? The psalm recalls several of the Lord’s deeds in the wilderness: parting the sea, the cloud by day, the fire by night, and bringing water from the rock.
Did you know? Manna is described as “grain from heaven,” and in the following verse it is also called “the bread of the mighty”; this emphasizes its heavenly origin and its provision for the people.
Did you know? Alongside its description of sins and punishments, the psalm emphasizes the Lord’s mercy: he forgives iniquity, repeatedly turns away his anger, and does not stir up all his wrath.

Did you know? In its description of the plagues of Egypt, the psalm mentions flies and frogs, and later locusts, hail, pestilence, and the plague of the firstborn; it presents them as a reminder of the Lord’s power.

Did you know? After describing the rebellion in the land, the psalm says that the Lord abandoned the tabernacle at Shiloh—a turning point in which the loss of the sacred place is connected to the people’s sins.
Did you know? At the end of the psalm, David is described as being taken from the sheepfolds to shepherd Jacob and Israel; his leadership is presented as a combination of integrity and wisdom.
